overview.intro: Confirmed attacks affected hospital care, online stores, surveillance cameras and personal data. Investigations are still determining the full scope of several incidents.

items.headline: New Mexico hospital diverts ambulances after cybersecurity incident
items.what_happened: The University of New Mexico Health System experienced a cybersecurity incident on Monday, October 26. Its main hospital stopped accepting some patients, more than 30 clinics canceled appointments, and classes were canceled. The FBI is assisting an active investigation.
items.impact: Ambulances were sent elsewhere, temporarily leaving New Mexico without an emergency department able to handle the most serious injuries. Hospitals and clinics began reopening in stages later Monday. The health system’s Level 1 trauma center was affected.
items.what_next: Watch for service-restoration notices and investigation updates from UNM. The cause, scope and any theft of patient, employee or student information remain under investigation.

items.headline: Hackers confirmed running commands through widely used website software
items.what_happened: Researchers confirmed successful attacks against decoy systems using two flaws in widely used PHP website software. The activity was recorded on October 24, after scanning and unsuccessful attempts had already been seen. The affected software versions were fixed October 21.
items.impact: This does not show that ordinary websites were compromised, but it raises the risk for websites still running affected versions. PHP supports a large share of websites, including services people use for shopping and information.
items.what_next: U.S. government agencies have until October 29 to apply fixes. Researchers are watching for attacks against real websites and for evidence that attackers downloaded additional malware.

items.headline: Nearly 1,000 online stores carry hidden code aimed at shoppers
items.what_happened: A campaign active since July 2025 infected 953 online stores, mostly using Magento. The stores were altered to load attacker-controlled code only for real visitors, helping it avoid security checks. The final harmful payload has not been identified.
items.impact: Shoppers may face redirects, scams or attempts to steal information, although the reporting does not confirm what the code ultimately did. Store owners may need to take sites offline while investigating, potentially delaying orders.
items.what_next: Researchers are checking whether the campaign is still spreading and what the hidden code delivers. Customers should be cautious if a store behaves unusually or asks for unexpected payment or account details.

items.headline: Ukraine warns that hackers are taking over connected security cameras
items.what_happened: Ukraine’s CERT-UA confirmed cases involving Dahua cameras and recorders. Attackers accessed video, changed settings and created accounts. The incidents were reported last week; the number of affected devices, targets and responsible group remain unknown.
items.impact: Compromised cameras could expose homes, businesses, government sites or military-related activity. The warning does not confirm that any particular public facility or military camera was affected.
items.what_next: Ukrainian authorities are investigating whether the activity connects to an earlier campaign that compromised more than 14,500 cameras between June and July. Camera owners may see service or viewing changes while systems are secured.

items.headline: University of Copenhagen says data on 525,000 people was accessed
items.what_happened: Hackers entered a university test environment containing personal information. The university detected the breach on October 20 and disclosed it on October 23. A later update added 20,000 staff and students whose building-access PINs may have been exposed.
items.impact: Names, national identity numbers, contact details and some access codes may be at risk. The university says daily operations were not disrupted and there is no indication that operational systems were accessed.
items.what_next: The university is still determining the full scope and is replacing access codes while reopening restricted areas. Affected people should be wary of convincing messages asking for information or access.

finance.intro: No confirmed banking or payment-system outage was reported. Online-store compromises create a possible shopping and payment risk, but theft was not confirmed.

items.headline: Compromised online stores may expose shoppers to scams
items.what_happened: Attackers planted hidden browser code on 953 online stores. It was designed to distinguish real shoppers from security scanners, but researchers have not captured the final payload.
items.impact: Customers could encounter redirects or attempts to collect payment or account details. The reports do not confirm stolen card data or payment failures.
items.what_next: Investigators are working to identify the final payload and remaining affected stores. Shoppers should verify unusual payment prompts through the store’s normal website or app.

healthcare.intro: A cybersecurity incident disrupted the largest hospital system in New Mexico. Separate healthcare data exposures affected plan members and patients, without reported care outages.

items.headline: New Mexico hospital resumes services in stages after cyber incident
items.what_happened: UNM Health System diverted ambulances, canceled appointments at more than 30 clinics and canceled classes on October 26. Hospitals and clinics later began reopening in phases.
items.impact: Emergency care and routine appointments were disrupted. Other New Mexico hospital systems accepted additional patients. The incident’s cause and data impact remain unclear.
items.what_next: Watch for service-restoration notices and investigation updates from UNM. The cause, scope and any theft of patient, employee or student information remain under investigation.

items.headline: Vendor access incident affects 238,083 Denver health-plan members
items.what_happened: A vendor’s access key was publicly exposed for more than a year and could have opened a read-only database containing Denver Health Medical Plan information. The plan has not found evidence that the key was misused.
items.impact: Names, dates of birth, eligibility, provider and health measurements may have been exposed. Financial details and Social Security numbers were not involved, and data could not be changed or deleted through the key.
items.what_next: Denver Health Medical Plan is notifying affected people while the investigation continues. Recipients should watch for targeted health-related scams or messages requesting account information.

internet.intro: Confirmed incidents included a hospital disruption, compromised websites, hacked cameras and exposed university data. No broad communications outage was reported.

items.headline: Hackers took over Dahua cameras in Ukraine
items.what_happened: CERT-UA reported unauthorized access to Dahua cameras and recorders, including viewing video, changing settings and adding accounts. The timing and number of affected devices are unknown.
items.impact: Private, business or government surveillance footage could be exposed. The report does not confirm effects on public internet or camera services.
items.what_next: Authorities are investigating the scope and whether it matches an earlier campaign affecting more than 14,500 devices. Further findings may clarify which owners are affected.

items.headline: University test system breach puts personal data at risk
items.what_happened: The University of Copenhagen confirmed unauthorized access to a test environment holding data on 525,000 people, later adding 20,000 people whose access PINs may have been exposed.
items.impact: Names, national identity numbers, contact details and some building-access information may be used for phishing or impersonation. University operations were not disrupted.
items.what_next: The university is replacing access codes and continuing its investigation. Affected students and staff should verify unexpected messages independently.

supply_chain.intro: A vendor-related healthcare data incident affected Denver Health members. This was an exposed supplier key, not a compromise of widely distributed software.

items.headline: Exposed vendor key may have opened Denver health-plan data
items.what_happened: SquareML, a healthcare analytics supplier, accidentally placed an access key on a public website in June 2025. Denver Health Medical Plan learned of the exposure on August 14, 2026, and disabled the key on August 18.
items.impact: The key could provide read-only access to information on 238,083 members. The plan found no evidence of misuse, and records could not be changed, deleted or exported through the key.
items.what_next: Denver Health is notifying affected members while the investigation continues. People receiving notices should be alert for health-insurance impersonation attempts.

overview.intro: New reports describe data exposure at a developer platform, repeated breaches involving UK police suppliers, customer information stolen from an energy company, and a hardware-wallet verification compromise. An international operation also cut criminals off from 180,000 infected computers. Several incidents caused no reported service outage.

items.headline: Warp says a vendor breach exposed some AI activity records
items.what_happened: Warp said an attack on a third-party vendor exposed agent decision logs and usage data for about 1% of its users. The incident was detected Friday, and outside investigators and law enforcement are involved.
items.impact: Warp has not said whether source code, prompts, passwords or other sensitive data were exposed. The company says it contained the incident and notified users it identified as affected. The platform has at least 800,000 users.
items.what_next: The investigation should clarify the affected users and the types of data exposed. Warp may provide further notices if more sensitive information is found.

items.headline: UK watchdog finds repeated breaches of suppliers holding police data
items.what_happened: A UK policing watchdog reported multiple cyberattacks since 2021 against suppliers that held police information. It did not identify the suppliers, count the attacks or confirm whether data was stolen.
items.impact: The report says some attacks affected operational systems, data or services, but the public impact of the supplier breaches is unclear. Police recorded 252 cybersecurity incidents in the first three months of 2026, plus 796 near misses.
items.what_next: The investigation and oversight work may clarify which police forces, suppliers and records were affected. The watchdog warned that further attacks are highly likely.

items.headline: Energy customers in France have data stolen through a partner platform
items.what_happened: Attackers accessed a marketing platform used by ENGIE’s business partners and stole customer information. ENGIE said the company’s internal systems were not breached and the incident is limited to customers in France.
items.impact: Names, addresses, contact details and energy contract information were exposed. No banking data was involved, and there is no report of power or gas service disruption.
items.what_next: ENGIE has contacted affected customers and notified authorities. Further details, including the number of people affected, may emerge from the investigation.

items.headline: Hardware-wallet maker replaces verification key after website breach
items.what_happened: Keystone said attackers obtained the key used to verify that its cryptocurrency hardware wallets are genuine, through a weakness in a third-party monitoring tool. Customer shipping records were also accessed.
items.impact: A counterfeit wallet using the old key could pass the online check and potentially steal cryptocurrency, but Keystone reported no counterfeit devices or thefts. The breach exposed records for 25,964 buyers and 12,873 abandoned checkouts; payment and bank details were not involved.
items.what_next: Keystone is destroying 18,835 unsold devices, replacing the verification key and contacting affected customers. Orders are paused while devices using the new key are prepared.

items.headline: Australia cuts malware criminals off from 180,000 infected computers
items.what_happened: Australia’s Signals Directorate gained access to a criminal control system for the Amadey malware and disconnected it from about 180,000 infected computers worldwide. The malware had been used to install more malware and steal account details.
items.impact: The criminals can no longer use that particular system to issue commands or steal new information from those computers. Earlier theft may still be misused, and the operation did not clean the infected devices.
items.what_next: Authorities may identify victims or related criminal infrastructure. People and organizations affected by the malware may continue receiving notifications as investigations develop.

overview.intro: New reports show a Japanese hosting provider confirming customer data exposure, a payment-data theft campaign through a shared shopping platform, and full recovery after Monday’s New Mexico hospital disruption.

items.headline: Japanese hosting provider confirms customer data was published online
items.what_happened: GMO Internet said attackers who entered its Onamae Desktop Cloud stole and published company and customer data. The intrusion was detected October 20. The provider had warned that malware might have been placed on up to 26,739 customer servers.
items.impact: Customer payment information was not exposed, but trading-account details and MetaTrader sign-in information may have been. GMO says ransomware was not activated on customer machines, although service availability was reduced while servers were shut down.
items.what_next: GMO is scanning customer systems, checking the leaked data and working with Trend Micro. It may offer further compensation and replace computers damaged by any later ransomware activity.

items.headline: Shared shopping-platform code stole card details from Brazilian shoppers
items.what_happened: Attackers altered an analytics script used by Convertr, a Brazilian online-shopping platform serving dozens of major brands. The script loaded on merchants’ checkout pages and collected card numbers, expiration dates, security codes, names and taxpayer numbers. The campaign was found October 24.
items.impact: Some shoppers who paid by card through affected Brazilian stores may have had payment details captured. This is a confirmed payment-data theft campaign, but the number of affected shoppers and any resulting fraud are unclear.
items.what_next: Convertr removed the harmful code and upgraded the affected software. It is notifying merchants and payment providers. Investigators may clarify which stores and transactions were exposed.

items.headline: New Mexico hospital says patient care has fully returned to normal
items.what_happened: After Monday’s cyberattack, UNM Health said all critical electronic systems were back online Tuesday. Hospitals reopened fully, ambulance traffic returned to normal, and clinics resumed scheduled appointments and procedures.
items.impact: The earlier ambulance diversion, canceled appointments and suspended surgeries have ended. UNM said the event affected some end-user devices but did not reach core systems or servers. Claims by a ransomware group about stolen data remain unconfirmed.
items.what_next: UNM and law enforcement are still investigating the cause and scope. Patients, staff and students may receive further notices if investigators confirm information exposure.

finance.intro: Confirmed payment-data theft affected a shared Brazilian shopping platform. A separate Japanese hosting incident may expose trading-account details, but no banking or payment data was reported stolen.

items.headline: Brazilian checkout script captured shoppers’ payment details
items.what_happened: A compromised analytics script used by Convertr-loaded online stores collected card information during checkout. Convertr removed the script after the campaign was identified October 24.
items.impact: Card payments made through some affected Brazilian stores may be exposed. Confirmed financial losses and the number of affected shoppers are not known.
items.what_next: Merchants and payment providers are being notified. Further investigation may identify affected stores and transactions.

items.headline: Japanese cloud-service customers warned about exposed trading credentials
items.what_happened: GMO Internet said attackers stole and published company and customer data after entering its Onamae Desktop Cloud service. Trading-account details and MetaTrader sign-in information may be included.
items.impact: No payment information was exposed, according to GMO. The company has not confirmed misuse of trading accounts, but customer servers experienced reduced availability during the response.
items.what_next: GMO is verifying the leaked information and scanning customer systems. More details about affected accounts and compensation may follow.

healthcare.intro: UNM Health reports that the service disruption from Monday’s cyberattack has ended. The investigation and any data-exposure assessment continue.

items.headline: New Mexico hospital restores ambulances, clinics and surgeries
items.what_happened: UNM Health said hospitals are fully open, ambulance traffic is normal and clinics have resumed scheduled care after Monday’s attack.
items.impact: The earlier diversion of ambulances and cancellation of appointments and outpatient surgeries have stopped. UNM says core systems and servers were not penetrated, but some end-user devices were affected.
items.what_next: Law enforcement and UNM are continuing to determine what happened and whether information was taken. Additional notices may be issued if the scope changes.

internet.intro: A Japanese hosting provider confirmed a customer-data leak and continuing recovery work. A separate shared checkout service was used to steal payment information from online shoppers.

items.headline: Japanese hosting provider confirms data leak after customer-server incident
items.what_happened: GMO Internet said data belonging to the company and its Onamae Desktop Cloud customers was published online after an October 20 intrusion. Up to 26,739 customer servers may have received malware, according to the company’s earlier warning.
items.impact: Service availability was reduced while servers were shut down and examined. GMO says payment information was not exposed, but trading credentials and account details may have been.
items.what_next: The company is scanning systems, checking the authenticity of leaked data and working with outside investigators. It says ransomware has not been activated on customer machines.

items.headline: Compromised checkout script affected stores using a shared platform
items.what_happened: Attackers changed Convertr’s analytics script so it collected information entered by shoppers on checkout pages. The code was removed after the campaign was identified October 24.
items.impact: Some online shoppers in Brazil may have had card and identity details stolen. The number of affected stores and customers is not yet known.
items.what_next: Convertr is notifying merchants and payment providers while investigators determine the campaign’s reach.

supply_chain.intro: Two incidents involved upstream services used by other organizations: a Japanese hosting provider and a shared Brazilian shopping platform. Both created risks beyond a single company’s own systems.

items.headline: GMO cloud service breach put customer servers and data at risk
items.what_happened: Attackers breached Onamae Desktop Cloud, a Japanese virtual-server provider, and may have placed malware on customer servers. GMO later confirmed that company and customer data was published online.
items.impact: Customers faced reduced service availability while servers were shut down. Trading credentials may have been exposed, but payment information was not, according to GMO.
items.what_next: GMO is examining customer systems and leaked information. The extent of customer impact and any further compensation remain under review.

items.headline: Convertr platform breach exposed shoppers across multiple stores
items.what_happened: A malicious change to Convertr’s shared analytics script reached checkout pages for merchants using the platform. The script stole payment and identity details entered by shoppers.
items.impact: This was a confirmed compromise of a shared service, not just one online store. Affected merchants and the number of exposed shoppers are still unclear.
items.what_next: Convertr removed the code and upgraded the affected software. Merchant and payment-provider investigations may establish the full scope.
